## Isogonal Conjugates and Humpty-Dumpty Points

::: {#lem-3point1}
## Trigonometric Ceva's Theorem
In $\triangle ABC$, let $X,Y,Z$ lie on segments $BC,CA,AB$, respectively. Then $AX,BY,CZ$ are concurrent if and only if
$$\frac{\sin\angle BAX\sin\angle CBY\sin\angle ACZ}{\sin\angle XAC\sin\angle YBA\sin\angle ZCB}=1$$
(if $X,Y,Z$ do not all lie on the segments, $AX,BY,CZ$ may instead be concurrent or parallel, or $X,Y,Z$ may be collinear).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows directly from Ceva's theorem and the Law of Sines.
:::

::: {#thm-3point1}
Let $\ell_A$ be the reflection of $AP$ across $AI$, and define $\ell_B,\ell_C$ analogously. Then $\ell_A,\ell_B,\ell_C$ concur at a single point $Q$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows immediately from @lem-3point1.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The point $Q$ in @thm-3point1 is called the **isogonal conjugate** of $P$.
:::

::: {#cor-3point1}
The isogonal conjugate of $I$ is $I$ itself.
:::

::: {#cor-3point2}
$O$ and $H$ are isogonal conjugates.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The isogonal conjugate of $G$ is the **symmedian point** (or **Lemoine point**) $X(6)$, denoted by $K$ unless otherwise stated. The line $AK$ is called the **$A$-symmedian**.
:::

::: {#lem-3point2}
$A$, $K$, and the intersection of the tangents to $(ABC)$ at $B$ and $C$ are collinear.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $A'$ be the reflection of $A$ across $M_{BC}$. Then the isogonal conjugate of $A'$ is the intersection $X$ of the tangents to $(ABC)$ at $B$ and $C$ (as can be seen by computing $\angle BCA'$ and $\angle CBA'$). Taking the isogonal conjugate of the median $AA'$ shows that $X$ lies on the $A$-symmedian.
:::

::: {#cor-3point3}
$Ge$ is the symmedian point of the contact triangle.
:::

::: {#lem-3point3}
If the $A$-symmedian intersects $(ABC)$ again at $D$, then $AB\cdot CD=AC\cdot BD$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let the tangents to $(ABC)$ at $B$ and $C$ intersect at $X$. By @lem-3point2, $A,D,X$ are collinear.

Since $\triangle XBD\stackrel{-}{\sim}\triangle XAB$ and $\triangle XCD\stackrel{-}{\sim}\triangle XAC$, we have
$$\frac{AB}{BD}=\frac{XA}{XB}=\frac{XA}{XC}=\frac{AC}{CD}.$$
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
A cyclic quadrilateral $PQRS$ satisfying $PQ\cdot RS=PS\cdot QR$ is called a **harmonic quadrilateral**.
:::

::: {#cor-3point4}
In a harmonic quadrilateral $PQRS$, the intersection of the tangents to its circumcircle at $Q$ and $S$ is collinear with $P$ and $R$.
:::

::: {#lem-3point4}
Using the notation of @lem-3point3, the center of spiral similarity sending $BA$ to $AC$ is $M_{AD}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Since $M_{AD}$ lies on $(XO)$, we have
$$\measuredangle M_{AD}BA=\measuredangle M_{AD}BC+\measuredangle CBA=\measuredangle M_{AD}XC+\measuredangle XCA=\measuredangle M_{AD}AC.$$
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The point $M_{AD}$ in @lem-3point4 is called the **$A$-Dumpty point**.
:::

::: {#lem-3point5}
If $T$ is the $A$-Dumpty point, then $(ATC)$ is tangent to $AB$ and $(ATB)$ is tangent to $AC$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Consider the degenerate complete quadrilateral $(BA,AA,AC,CB)$; the result follows from @thm-1point2 and @cor-1point1.
:::

::: {#lem-3point6}
Let $(P,P')$ and $(Q,Q')$ be pairs of isogonal conjugates. If $P,Q,B,C$ are concyclic, then $P',Q',B,C$ are also concyclic.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows immediately by angle chasing.
:::

::: {#cor-3point5}
If $P$ and $P'$ are isogonal conjugates, then the isogonal conjugate of $(BPC)$ is $(BP'C)$. In particular, the isogonal conjugate of $(BIC)$ is itself.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The isogonal conjugate of the $A$-Dumpty point is called the **$A$-Humpty point**.
:::

::: {#lem-3point7}
The $A$-Humpty point lies on both $(BHC)$ and the $A$-median.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By @cor-3point5, the isogonal conjugate of $(BOC)$ is $(BHC)$.

Since the $A$-Dumpty point lies on $(BOC)$ and the $A$-symmedian, its isogonal conjugate—the $A$-Humpty point—lies on $(BHC)$ and the $A$-median.
:::

::: {#lem-3point8}
If $S$ is the $A$-Humpty point, then $(ASC)$ and $(ASB)$ are both tangent to $BC$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows from @lem-3point5 and @lem-3point6 (and its limiting case).
:::

::: {#lem-3point9}
Using the notation of @lem-3point3 and @lem-3point8, the reflection of $S$ across $BC$ is $D$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By @lem-3point7, $S$ lies on the $A$-median and $(HBC)$.

By @lem-1point6, the reflection of $S$ across $M_{BC}$ lies on $(ABC)$, so it is the second intersection of the $A$-median with $(ABC)$.

Consequently, the reflection of $S$ across $BC$ is the intersection $D$ of the $A$-symmedian with $(ABC)$.
:::

::: {#lem-3point10}
Using the notation of @lem-3point6, if $B,C,P,Q$ are concyclic, then $\triangle APQ\stackrel{-}{\sim}\triangle AP'Q'$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By @lem-3point6, $B,C,P',Q'$ are concyclic. Let $AP$ and $AP'$ intersect $(BCP)$ and $(BCP')$ again at $R$ and $R'$, respectively.

By @cor-3point5, $R$ and $R'$ are isogonal conjugates. Angle chasing then gives
$$\measuredangle APQ=\measuredangle RPQ=\measuredangle RBQ=\measuredangle Q'BR'=\measuredangle Q'P'R'=\measuredangle Q'P'A,$$
and similarly $\measuredangle AQP=\measuredangle AQ'P'$, proving the opposite similarity.
:::

::: {#lem-3point11}
The $A$-Humpty point lies on $(AH)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Using the notation of @lem-3point5 and @lem-3point8, @lem-3point10 gives $\triangle ASO\stackrel{-}{\sim}\triangle ATH$.

Therefore, $\measuredangle ATH=\measuredangle OSA=90^\circ$ (or equivalently, $\measuredangle ASH=\measuredangle ATO=90^\circ$).
:::

::: {#lem-3point12}
Let $B_{\perp AC}=E$ and $C_{\perp AB}=F$. Then $M_{BC}E$, $M_{BC}F$, and the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ are all tangent to $(AH)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Since $A,H,E,F$ and $B,C,E,F$ are concyclic, the result follows immediately by angle chasing.
:::

::: {#lem-3point13}
Using the notation of @lem-3point8 and @lem-3point12, $AESF$ is a harmonic quadrilateral.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows from @lem-3point3, @lem-3point7, and @lem-3point12.
:::

::: {#lem-3point14}
Let $(AH)$ intersect $(ABC)$ again at $N$. Using the notation of @lem-3point8 and @lem-3point12, the lines $AN, HS, EF, BC$ are concurrent.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Considering the radical center of $(AH)$, $(ABC)$, and $(BC)$ together with the radical center of $(AH)$, $(HBC)$, and $(ABC)$ shows that all four lines pass through a common point.
:::

::: {#cor-3point6}
Using the notation of @lem-3point14, the orthocenter of $\triangle AHM_{BC}$ is $EF\cap BC$.
:::

::: {#cor-3point7}
Let $S_A$ and $T_A$ be the $A$-Humpty and $A$-Dumpty points, and define $S_B,S_C,T_B,T_C$ analogously. Then $S_A,S_B,S_C$ all lie on $(HG)$, and $T_A,T_B,T_C$ all lie on $(OK)$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
If a point $P$ satisfies $\measuredangle PAB=\measuredangle PBC=\measuredangle PCA=\omega$, then $P$ is called the **first Brocard point**, its isogonal conjugate is called the **second Brocard point**, and $\omega$ is called the **Brocard angle**.
:::

::: {#cor-3point8}
Let $Br$ and $Br'$ denote the first and second Brocard points, respectively. Then $(BrAC)$ is tangent to $AB$, and $(Br'AB)$ is tangent to $AC$.
:::

::: {#lem-3point15}
Using the notation of @cor-3point8, $Br$ and $Br'$ lie on $(OK)$, and $OK$ is the perpendicular bisector of $BrBr'$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Using the notation of @cor-3point7, @lem-3point5 implies that $A,C,T_A,Br$ and $A,B,T_A,Br'$ are concyclic.

Thus
$$
\measuredangle BrT_AA=\measuredangle BrCA=\omega=\measuredangle AT_ABr',
$$
so
$$
\measuredangle BrT_ABr'=2\omega=\measuredangle BrT_BBr'=\measuredangle BrT_CBr'.
$$
By @cor-3point7, $Br,Br',T_A,T_B,T_C$ all lie on $(OK)$.

Furthermore, $\measuredangle BrT_AK=\measuredangle BrT_AA=\omega=\measuredangle KT_ABr'$, so arcs $KBr$ and $KBr'$ on $(OK)$ are equal.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The line $OK$ is called the **Brocard axis**, and the circle $(OK)$ is called the **Brocard circle**.
:::

::: {#lem-3point16}
Using the notation of @lem-3point15, the intersections $BBr\cap CBr'$, $CBr\cap ABr'$, and $ABr\cap BBr'$ (which lie on the perpendicular bisectors of $BC,CA,AB$, respectively) all lie on the Brocard circle, and the triangle they form is oppositely similar to $\triangle ABC$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $P=BBr\cap CBr'$.

By @lem-3point15, a point $X$ lies on $(OK)$ if and only if $\measuredangle BrXBr'=2\omega$.

Hence $P$ lies on $(OK)$, and $OP\perp BC$.

It follows that $KP\parallel BC$, and the opposite similarity is immediate by angle chasing.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The triangle in @lem-3point16 is called the **first Brocard triangle**.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The triangle formed by the feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ to the sidelines of $\triangle ABC$ is called the **pedal triangle** of $P$, and its circumcircle is called the **pedal circle** of $P$.
:::

::: {#thm-3point2}
## Reim's Theorem
Let circles $\omega$ and $\Omega$ intersect at $A$ and $B$. Let lines $\ell_A$ and $\ell_B$ pass through $A$ and $B$, respectively, with $\ell_A$ intersecting $\omega$ and $\Omega$ again at $P$ and $P'$, and $\ell_B$ intersecting $\omega$ and $\Omega$ again at $Q$ and $Q'$. Then $PQ\parallel P'Q'$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows immediately by angle chasing, or by considering the power of $\ell_A\cap\ell_B$.
:::

::: {#lem-3point17}
If $\measuredangle XAB=\measuredangle CAY$, then the four feet $X_{\perp AB}$, $X_{\perp AC}$, $Y_{\perp AB}$, and $Y_{\perp AC}$ are concyclic.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $X'$ be the reflection of $X$ across $AI$. By symmetry, the four feet from $X$ and $X'$ to $AB$ and $AC$ are concyclic.

Since $A,X',Y$ are collinear, the segments joining the feet from $X'$ and $Y$ to $AB$ and $AC$ are parallel; the result then follows from @thm-3point2.
:::

::: {#lem-3point18}
The pedal circles of two isogonal conjugates $P$ and $Q$ coincide, and their common center is $M_{PQ}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By @lem-3point17, we obtain three cyclic quadruples of pedal projections. If their circumcircles did not coincide, their pairwise radical axes $AB,BC,CA$ would be concurrent, a contradiction.

Moreover, $M_{PQ}$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $P_{\perp BC}Q_{\perp BC}$, and similarly for the other two sides, so $M_{PQ}$ is the center of this circle.
:::

::: {#lem-3point19}
Let $P$ and $Q$ be isogonal conjugates. Then the circumcircle of the reflections of $P$ across the three sidelines of $\triangle ABC$ has center $Q$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Applying a homothety centered at $P$ with ratio $2$ to @lem-3point18 yields the result.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Let $A_\alpha$ lie on $BC$ such that $\measuredangle PA_\alpha B=\alpha$, and define $B_\alpha,C_\alpha$ analogously. Then $(A_\alpha B_\alpha C_\alpha)$ is called the **$\alpha$-pedal circle** of $P$.
:::

::: {#lem-3point20}
If $P$ and $Q$ are isogonal conjugates, then the $\alpha$-pedal circle of $P$ coincides with the $(-\alpha)$-pedal circle of $Q$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows by the same concyclicity argument as in @lem-3point17 and @lem-3point18.
:::

::: {#lem-3point21}
Suppose a circle $\Gamma$ intersects $BC$ at $A_1,A_2$, $CA$ at $B_1,B_2$, and $AB$ at $C_1,C_2$. Then the Miquel points $P$ and $Q$ associated with $\triangle A_1B_1C_1$ and $\triangle A_2B_2C_2$ in @lem-1point1 are isogonal conjugates.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By angle chasing, there exists an angle $\alpha$ such that $(A_1B_1C_1)$ is the $\alpha$-pedal circle of $P$.

By @lem-3point20, $(A_1B_1C_1)$ is also the $(-\alpha)$-pedal circle of the isogonal conjugate $P'$ of $P$.

Angle chasing then shows that $A,B_2,C_2,P'$ are concyclic, and similarly for the other vertices, so $P'=Q$.
:::
